hook.support: You have one minute. You have an idea. Can you get someone to say yes? That is a pitch.
hook.core: Sixty seconds. One idea. A room of people who’ve heard a hundred pitches today. Can you make them lean in? Whether it’s a business idea, a fundraiser or yourself in a job interview, a pitch is how you get a yes.
hook.extend: A pitch is promotion in its most compressed form: a spoken, structured case for an idea, delivered to an audience with the power to say yes. It tests language choice, structure and delivery all at once.

why.support: Pitching helps you sell an idea, a product or yourself.
why.core: You’ll pitch all your life: for jobs, for money, for support. A clear, confident pitch can open doors.
why.extend: Pitching is a core work skill in business, trades, community work and job interviews. Being able to persuade out loud, in a short time, is rare and valued.

articles.title: Sixty seconds to yes

body.support:
A **pitch** is a short talk. You use it to get someone to say yes to your idea.

**A pitch has five parts:**
- **Hook:** grab their attention. Ask a question, or say something surprising.
- **Problem:** what is wrong or missing?
- **Solution:** your idea, and how it fixes the problem.
- **Proof:** why it will work. Did people like it? Did you test it?
- **The ask:** what do you want? Money? Help? A yes?
.
**How to say it:**
- Look at the people you’re talking to.
- Speak loud and clear.
- Stand still. Don’t sway.
- Smile. Look like you believe it.
- Pause before your ask.
.
**Practise.** Say it out loud five times. Time it. Cut anything you don’t need.
body.core:
A **pitch** is a short, spoken case for an idea. You might pitch a business to an **investor**, a fundraiser to your principal, or yourself to an employer.

**Structure: five parts in 60 seconds**
- **Hook (5–10 sec):** a question, a surprising fact or a quick story. “Who here has eaten a cold pie at the footy?”.
- **Problem (10 sec):** make it real for the listener.
- **Solution (15 sec):** your idea, in plain words. What it is, who it’s for, how it works.
- **Proof (15 sec):** why it will work: you tested it, people paid, you have the skills.
- **The ask (10 sec):** exactly what you want. “$300 to buy a pie warmer.”.

**Words that work:**
- Say “you”: talk to the listener.
- Use short sentences and strong verbs.
- Give one number that sticks.
.
**Delivery:**
- **Eye contact** around the whole panel.
- a confident, warm **tone**: not shouting, not mumbling.
- **body language:** stand still, feet apart, hands open.
- a pause before your ask, so it lands.

**Know your setting.** A bank manager wants numbers, in a formal style. A crowd at a market wants energy and fun. Same idea, different words.
body.extend:
A **pitch** is a compressed, spoken argument for an idea, aimed at someone who can say yes. Entrepreneurs pitch to **investors**, community groups pitch to councils, and job seekers pitch themselves.

**Structure.** A 60-second pitch usually moves through five beats:
- **hook:** a question, statistic or short story that creates curiosity.
- **problem:** a concrete pain point the audience recognises.
- **solution:** what your idea is, for whom, and how it works.
- **proof:** evidence it will succeed, such as testing, early sales, skills or support.
- **the ask:** a specific request, with a number if possible.

**Language that influences.**
- direct address (“you”) and inclusive language (“we”).
- concrete, vivid nouns and active verbs.
- one memorable figure rather than a list of statistics.
- rhetorical questions in the hook, and a clear, confident close.

**Delivery.** Oral communication carries as much weight as content:
- sustained **eye contact** across the panel.
- a confident **tone**, with **intonation** that rises with energy and falls to signal certainty.
- open, still **body language**.
- a deliberate pause before the ask.

**Setting.** Adjust register to context. An investor panel expects formality and figures. A market crowd responds to energy and humour. A job interview needs warmth and evidence.

caseStudies.title: The pitch that heard “no” 100 times

body.support:
**Melanie Perkins** grew up in **Perth**. At uni, she taught students how to use design programs. She saw that the programs were hard to use.

She had an idea. What if design was easy, and online?

She and **Cliff Obrecht** started small. They made a website for schools to design yearbooks.

Then they wanted to build something bigger. They needed money. So they **pitched** to **investors**.

Most said **no**. Melanie says she heard “no” more than **100 times**.

After each no, she changed her pitch. She made it better.

In **2013**, they launched **Canva**. Today, people all over the world use it.
body.core:
**Melanie Perkins** was a university student in **Perth**, teaching others how to use design software. She noticed the programs were hard to learn and expensive. Her idea: simple design tools, online, for everyone.

With **Cliff Obrecht**, she started small, with an online tool for designing school yearbooks. To build the bigger idea, they needed **investors**.

Perkins has said they were rejected by more than **100** investors. Some doubted the idea. Some doubted a tech company could grow from Australia.

She has said she changed her pitch after **every** meeting. Each “no” showed her what wasn’t working.

In **2013**, they launched **Canva**. It became one of Australia’s best-known tech companies, used around the world.

The idea didn’t change much. The pitch did.
body.extend:
**Melanie Perkins** was a university student in **Perth** who taught design software to other students. She saw that it was difficult and expensive to learn, and imagined simple, online design tools for everyone.

With co-founder **Cliff Obrecht**, she first built an online tool for designing school yearbooks. To fund the larger vision, they had to persuade **investors**.

Perkins has said more than **100** investors turned them down. They faced doubts about the market, and about building a global tech company from Australia.

By her account, she revised her pitch deck after every meeting, more than a hundred times in a year. She treated each rejection as feedback on her structure, evidence and language.

**Canva** launched in **2013** and grew into one of Australia’s best-known technology companies.

The “100 rejections” figure comes from Perkins’ own retellings, not investor records. Even so, the story shows how much a pitch can change while the core idea stays the same.

model.text:
“Who here has walked past a park full of rubbish and done nothing?
Me too. In our town, the skate park bins overflow every weekend.
Our idea: Bin Squad. Year 11 students empty and clean the skate park bins every Sunday morning.
We tested it for three weekends. The park stayed clean, and two skaters joined us.
[pause] We’re asking the council for $150 for gloves, grabbers and bin bags.
Clean park. Proud town. Thank you.”

teacher.overview: Students learn the five-part structure of a 60-second pitch (hook, problem, solution, proof, ask), language choices that influence, and delivery (eye contact, tone, intonation, body language, pause before the ask). They adjust style for different settings and pitch to a panel. The case study is Melanie Perkins and Canva: by her account, more than 100 investor rejections, with the pitch revised after every meeting, before Canva launched in 2013.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 hook (a question the audience can answer); 2 real, local problem; 3 plain-words solution; 4 proof from a survey; 5 exact ask after a pause; 6 short, memorable close.

**Sort:** bank — thank you for your time; costs and prices; loan of $2,000. Market — free taste; hands up for hot chips; three for ten bucks.

**Case study:** design software was hard and expensive to learn; investors doubted the market and an Australian base; she revised the pitch after every meeting; Canva launched in 2013. Extend: the “100” figure comes from Perkins’ own accounts.

realityCheck: **Speaking anxiety is real.** Let students pitch to a small panel first, or use the video option; both meet the outcome.
**“Shark Tank” framing works,** but keep panel feedback kind and specific (use the rubric).
**Students may want to pitch themselves for a job.** That’s a great choice; the five parts still apply.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Pitch day has energy; time limits keep it moving.
